content.title: Reply to R5 (RE9a)
content.comment:
Thank you for recognizing the merit of our approach. 

**R5.1.** The proposed approach is straightforward (not a demerit), and is a native extension on how to extend the DETR into few-shot, although there exist some specific mechanism designs in this paper to facilitate such extension. However, similar ideas also can be found in existing papers such as [1], which appeared in 2021 in arXiv and published in 2022. Since [1] is already published, it should be included as a fair baseline to compare with and discuss and [1] should be the most close research reported in few-shot object detection. However, the performance reported in this manuscript seems is not as high as in [1] with a significant margin.

**A5.1.** The only resemblance with Meta-DETR is the use of the DETR architecture which is not claimed as a contribution in our paper.
We are using a set of templates as prompts, concatenated with the object queries that are jointly processed by the decoder - Meta-DETR learns a correlation module that generates a set of task encodings. These encodings will then serve as “classes”. In contrast, our objective is completely different as we are trying to predict the pseudo-class baked in the  “stamped” learnable embeddings (see contributions for details). 
Moreover our method doesn’t require fine tuning, while Meta-DETR does, hence they don’t fall in the same sub-area.

As Meta-DETR requires fine tuning on the novel classes, their results are not directly comparable with ours.  Despite this difference in settings, we would like to mention that for low-shot our results are comparable and even better, example:

VOC (set 2):

Shots: 1 2 3 5 10

Meta-detr: 27.9; 32.3; 38.4; 43.2; 51.8 

Ours: 37.3; 41.3; 43.4; 46.6; 49.0;

We will add these comparisons to the tables.


**R5.2.** From the data in Table 4, it indicates that the unsupervised pretraining is a key factor on the performance gain. However, there is no detailed discussion on the unsupervised pretraining in the main paper, which might be a problem. In fact, compared with ablation study of Table 5, the unsupervised pretraining is much more important than other modules presented in this paper. Therefore, I will suggest on focusing more on the pretraining method in the main paper.

**A5.2.** Thank you for your suggestion. We were a bit constrained in space. We will follow your suggestion and move as much as possible to the main paper.

**R5.3.** I also cannot very agree with three “desiderata” claimed by the authors (although this is not a serious issue). In standard few-shot object detection, fine-tuning or re-training is not an evil. Moreover, “without re-training” is a merit to all attention-based few-shot approaches, not a unique merit of this approach. The second point, “an arbitrary number of novel objects” actually is not even an issue for those “re-training” few-shot methods. And the "re-training" based method may also have the merit that it no need to require the "queries" for the detection on both base and novel classes, and the selection of "queries" may also affect the performance of the detection performance.

**A5.3.** We agree it is not an evil but it is limiting for some applications so if can be avoided it would be much better. Secondly, we never claimed that our method is the only ony that doesn’t perform re-training (see table 1). 

**R5.4.** In fact, many few-shot research is also focusing on the performance on both base and novel classes. One another important “desiderata” should be it can eliminate the performance drop as much as possible on base classes when adapting to novel classes. However, in this paper (similar for most "retraining-free" FS methods), the base class performance is not focused totally, and no experiment statistics are provided at all, this would be a problem to compare with most few-shot methods. Since the attention-based approach relying on the "queries", it's base-class performance may be worse than the "retraining" methods?

**A5.4.** The performance on the base classes is comparable with that of DETR supervised for large values of K (i.e. 10), which isn’t an issue for the base classes as we are assuming a large number of samples per class anyway.

We hope that we have addressed your remaining concerns and convinced you to upgrade the score. We are more than happy to provide any additional clarifications, should they be requested.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a transformer-based few-shot detection architecture to improve the few-shot performance without fine-tuning. Specifically, the model is firstly unsupervised pre-trained on ImageNet100 and the base dataset of COCO instead of supervised pretrained on the entire ImageNet. The model is then supervised trained on the corresponding base dataset, with the proposed pseudo-class embedding, multi-head cross-attention, and type-specific MLP
. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated on two few-shot benchmarks, PASCAL VOC and MS-COCO, and compared to its baseline.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
* The proposed method is simple and easy to understand and follow.
* The performance of the proposed method outperforms other FSOD without re-training methods.


Weaknesses:
* In 4.1 Results on PASCAL VOC the author claims " the author claims for k = 1, 2, i.e. on extreme few-shot settings, our method outperforms all re-training-based methods but DeFRCN^*". However, in Table 1 SRR-FSD and Zhang et al. are higher, and [1] is even higher.
* Compared with other fine-tuning methods, FS-DETR needs an extra unsupervised pre-training stage, which introduces a higher time cost compared with a simple fine-tuning step as in [1], [2]. For a practical FSOD system, does it violates a criterion that the system can be fast adapted to new categories?
* In Appendix B, the author claims "pre-training data used in the proposed work doesn’t offer any advantage over prior art approaches that use fully supervised pre-trained backbones". content.title: Reply to R4 (DR2c)
content.comment:
We thank you for your time and recognizing both the performance of our method and its ease to follow. We hope that we addressed your concerns below.

**R4.1.** In 4.1 Results on PASCAL VOC the author claims " the author claims for k = 1, 2, i.e. on extreme few-shot settings, our method outperforms all re-training-based methods but DeFRCN^*". However, in Table 1 SRR-FSD and Zhang et al. are higher, and [1] is even higher.

**A4.1.** Thank you we will correct this. Note, that our approach is the best performing one when no finetuning is used, which is the main target scenario of our work.

**R4.2.** Compared with other fine-tuning methods, FS-DETR needs an extra unsupervised pre-training stage, which introduces a higher time cost compared with a simple fine-tuning step as in [1], [2]. For a practical FSOD system, does it violates a criterion that the system can be fast adapted to new categories?

**A4.2.** Thank you for your question. It doesn’t violate the criteria, as the training is done only once. We have a discussion on this in appendix, section B.

**R4.3.** In Appendix B, the author claims "pre-training data used in the proposed work doesn’t offer any advantage over prior art approaches that use fully supervised pre-trained backbones". Table 6 demonstrates this point. However, I have some doubts about Table 6. Why initialization from Swav achieves the same performance as the proposed pre-training method on PASCAL VOC Split1? Now that initialization from a full supervised ImageNet pre-training achieves higher performance, what is the meaning of the proposed unsupervised-training method? Besides, how about unsupervised pretrained without the base COCO dataset but using the entire ImageNet?

**A4.3.** We believe there may be some misinterpretation of our results.  What we compare there is: backbone (the R50) pretrained using SwAV + our pretraining vs ImageNet Supervised + our pretraining. The first case is what we use for our approach, as we don’t use any form of supervision at any of stages, unlike prior work. It’s NOT possible to ONLY use backbone pretraining. This doesn’t work almost at all (see Table 4 for this results).
There are many data combinations that can be used, but due to limited resources, we had to restrict ourselves to the current data setting, especially as ImageNet has x10 more samples that its smaller set used.

**R4.4.** In my understanding, since the shape of the pseudo-class embedding is mk*d, which limits the model to detect most m classes. For the PASCAL VOC benchmark there are 15 base classes and 5 novel classes, now let's assume a scenario that the novel classes are enlarged to 6 classes, the fine-tuning-based methods can fast adapt to the newly enlarged dataset by simply fine-tuning the box predictor, but FS-DETR seems need re-training the whole model, is my understanding correct?

**R4.4.** The number of samples at test time can vary and it's not restricted to a predefined number of classes. If m grows too large (not the case for the current datasets), batching can be used.

We hope that we addressed your concerns and convinced you to raise your score. We are happy to reply to any additional clarifications, where needed.

content.title: Reply to R2 (F3H1) - part 1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for acknowledging the efficacy of our method. We hope that we have addressed all your concerns below

**R2.1.** On limited novelty, missing related works (Meta-DETR [2], TSF[3]) The novelty is limited and some closely related works are missing in the current version. First, there are some few-shot object detection works (e.g. [1]) that have supported novel class detection without fine-tuning. Second, Meta-DETR [2] is a few-shot object detection work and it also uses DETR architecture. Third, the authors think that pseudo-class embedding is a key contribution but lacks any discussions and experimental support. Furthermore, similar ideas of pseudo-class embedding have been presented in [3] (called semantic filter). In short, the above components are considered key contributions but they have been proposed in these recent works [1,2,3], and thus the novelty is limited. I strongly suggest that the authors sufficiently discuss the differences between the proposed method and these related works, especially Meta-DETR[2] and TSF[3].

**A2.1 (part I)** We politely disagree. As we show right below, our method has only superficial similarities with [1,2,3] mentioned in your review.  Moreover, where comparison is possible, we show that our method significantly outperforms them. Finally, we note that per ICLR policy we were not obliged to include comparisons with [1] and [3] as they were published at ECCV 2022, which took place after the ICLR deadline ([3] was even added on arxiv on **2nd of november 2022**). Nevertheless, by no means, we want to avoid the comparisons with these works please see below: 

First of all, we would like to re-state the **novelties** of our approach:
- We propose the very first, to the best of our knowledge, Few-Shot DEtection TRansformer (FS-DETR) capable of detecting multiple novel objects at once, supporting a variable number of samples per class, and without requiring any fine-tuning.

- We show that all these features can be enabled by extending DETR based on two key ideas: (1) feed the provided visual templates of novel classes as visual prompts during test time,and (2) “stamp” these prompts with pseudo-class embeddings, which are then predicted at the output of the decoder along with bounding boxes.

- We also propose a simple and efficient yet powerful pipeline consisting of unsupervised pre-training followed by prompt-like base class training.

*Please see part 2 of our answer for comparisons with with previous works.*

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1278 by Reviewer F3H1

content.title: Reply to R2 (F3H1) - part 2
content.comment:
**A2.1 (part II - continuation)**

Comparisons with previous works you mentioned:

- On Meta-DETR: The only resemblance with Meta-DETR is the use of the DETR architecture which is not claimed as a contribution in our paper.
We are using a set of templates as prompts, concatenated with the object queries that are jointly processed by the decoder - Meta-DETR learns a correlation module that generates a set of task encodings. These encodings will then serve as “classes”. In contrast, our objective is completely different as we are trying to predict the pseudo-class baked in the  “stamped” learnable embeddings (see contributions for details). 
Moreover our method doesn’t require fine tuning, while Meta-DETR does, hence they don’t fall in the same sub-area.

- On AirDet: there’s little to no similarity of our work with AirDet in terms of methodology, architecture etc. Our method is based on template prompting, via attention. The model is trained using a class agnostic loss, based on permutations where the goal is to predict the associated embeddings that serve the role of pseudo-classes when “stamped” to the prompts. Additionally, our work doesn't have, nor require, an explicit object proposal network. Meanwhile, AirDet, attempts to learn a set of prototypes and a cross-scale support guided proposal network, making the association and regression at the very end of model, instead of having it as part of the architecture directly as in our case.
Moreover, we do not claim that our method is the first method that supports few-shot detection without fine-tuning. See for example our table 1, where we compare with multiple such methods. 

- On TSF: TSF trains with completely different objectives: they use a multi-task loss where they combine a “rotation classifier”, “a metric classifier” and “a global classifier”. Moreover their architecture is based generally on a faster rcnn framework, using an external object proposal model, requires fine tuning and requires learning an additional transformer based semantic filter.

Moreover our approach, conceptually and implementation wise is completely different from the tsf module: tsf, performs attention between Q=f (the inp features) and Q=V= $\theta$, where $\theta$ is a learnable set of parameters. Its goal is to map f to f', transforming the features according to the whole dataset-wide learned information  by the trainable parameters $\theta$. In contrast, ours is fully dynamic (interactions between data and data as opposed to data and parameters), doesn't aim at transforming the input features f, but instead its using them to guide the detection outputs (predictions) directly, in a joint unified network, as opposed to having an external module as in tsf.

In light of the above, we hope that we have convinced you that  the resemblances you have identified with previous work are superficial.

Our work outperforms AirDet (without fine tuning) while matching and surpassing (for low-shot) even the performance of AirDet with fine tuning (COCO):

Shots (k=1): 1; 2; 3; 5;

AitDet (without fine tuning): 10.52;  12.02; 12.95; 14.28;

AirDet (with fine tuning): 11.40; 16.24; 19.39; 20.75;

Ours: 13.6; 17.5; 18.5; 20.5; 

The other 2 methods, Meta-DETR and tsf, don’t report results for no-finetuning so a direct comparison is not possible (we will add them to table 1). Despite this difference in settings, we would like to mention that for low-shot our results are comparable and even better, example:

VOC (set 2):

Shots: 1 2 3 5 10

tsf: 31.5; 39.3; 47.0; 52.1; 47.3

Meta-detr: 27.9; 32.3; 38.4; 43.2; 51.8

content.title: Reply to R2 (F3H1) - part 3
content.comment:
**R2.2.** It is not clear about the inference pipeline for me. Note that, the shape of template features and pseudo-class embedding is , where m is the number of classes and k is the number of support instances. However, the number of testing classes may not match that of training classes and I would like to know more details at the inference stage.

**A2.2.** Our model can support a dynamic number of input queries, meaning for reasonable values of m and k, this isn’t an issue.

**R2.3.** Compared to Meta-DETR, what is the advantage of the proposed method?

**A2.3.** Our method can be adopted to novel classes without any extra finetuning. In contrast, Meta-DETR requires fine tuning. As this is prone to overfitting, Meta-DETR has to be trained with both base and novel classes jointly. As a consequence, adding a new class requires re-training across all classes in their case. Moreover, our framework is simpler, as we don’t require training any additional correlation aggregation module.

**R2.4.** In my opinion, the proposed method may achieve a better performance if we fine-tune it on novel class data. Similar to [1], I would like to see the fine-tuning results and comparisons with other methods.

**A2.4.** Thank you for your suggestion. As mentioned in the introduction and the title of our paper, the main objective of our method is to provide a strong fine-tuning free approach for zero-shot detection. 
On COCO we are already outperforming [1] + fine tuning, for low-shot, without doing any finetuning, while almost matching their performance for higher-shot. While its reasonable assumption that performance will improve, devising the right finetuning strategy goes beyond the scope of our work. 

**R2.5.** The organization and writing need to be further improved. For example, it may be more reasonable if we place Eq. 2 into the FS-Decoder part.

**A2.5.** We believe that generally our paper is well organized. We are happy however to take into consideration any suggestions you may have, including this one. Thank you. 

**R2.6.** Some important components are not well ablated, for example, pseudo-class embedding (Eq. 1). I would like to see the results with and without the pseudo-class embedding, and the effects of hyper-parameters (for example, is set to 1).

**A2.6.**  We did ablate all the main components. It’s not possible to train our method without the pseudo-class embedding, as the loss depends on it. 

Setting k=1 is already “ablated” and it's not a hyper-parameter.This is how the results for 1-shot recognition are obtained. k represents the number of shots (templates) per class.

**R2.7.** In Table 4, we can see that the pre-trained backbone has a huge impact on the detection performance. Are the performance improvements consistent using the same backbone as other few-shot object detection methods (for example, ResNet-101 pre-trained on ImageNet)?

**A2.7.** We have no reason to believe this not to be the case. As our approach involves a pre-training strategy, due to tight resource constraints we focused our efforts on ResNet-50.  Note that pre-training in Table 4 refers to our pretraining strategy applied on top of a Resnet-50 model trained using SwAV. The model that underperforms there is still pre-trained using SwAV, but doesn’t use our proposed training objective, described at the end of Section 4 and appendix.

We hope that we have addressed all your concerns. We will include all the comparisons suggested. We would like to highlight that we outperform all of them in the without fine-tuning setting, which is the setting of our paper. We are more than happy to address any additional questions that may arise and we hope you can now recommend our work for acceptance. Thank you for your time and feedback.

content.title: Reply to R1 (BuJR)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for appreciating the novelty of our method. We hope that we addressed any remaining concerns bellow.

**R1.1.** The method implements FS-DETR with pre-trained DETR without supervision. This method of pre-training DETR is similar with DETReg method. It is interesting to explain the differences between this pre-training method and DETReg.

**A1.1.** Some of the key differences are:

- DETReg splits the object queries into groups, one group per template, then sums the extracted patch/template to the object queries of the corresponding groups. The objective is then to predict whether the patch is present within that group or not. As the number of templates searched grows, their performance degrades as there are not sufficient object queries per template. In contrast, the object queries and the templates are independent, as our approach is more akin to promoting.

- Our approach uses a different loss for pre-training (the permutation based) vs simple 0/1 classification.

- Our approach uses both positive (patches present in the image) and negative (patches not present in the image). This forces the model to learn to better identify which patch is present and which not.

We will add these details to the updated manuscript.

**R.1.2.** In Table 1 and Table 2, FS-DETR achieves SOTA without re-training methods. Is this because FS-DETR uses an additional template from the novel class? What about the performance when FS-DETR did not use this template? An ablation experiment is needed to demonstrate the effectiveness of novel class templates.

**A1.2.** Table 1 reports results of k-shot evaluation, hence all methods use k-samples (i.e. templates). Our method doesn’t use additional samples compared with prior work. It’s not possible to run our method, nor any of the other methods that don’t require pre-training without a template, as this will imply a zero-shot evaluation. 

**R.1.3.** In practical application, it is needed to detect objects in real-time, so test time is very important. Due to the novel class template being used as extra visual prompts, whether does FS-DETR compete with other previous methods in test time and memory consumption?

**A1.3.** The template can be cached during subsequent runs. The number of templates (typically 15-20) is small relative to that of the  number of object queries (300), therefore the runtime performance is not very different from that of a vanilla C-DETR. We measured approx. a 10% slowdown for our approach vs C-DETR, which we believe to be competitive.

**R1.4.**  What is the ratio between the number of novel class templates and the number of novel classes (test sets)? Does one novel class correspond to one template image, and the number of templates affect the experimental results?

**A1.4.** During the pre-training we have as many classes as there are proposals across imagenet, as each proposal is in essence treated as a class. During the adaptation stage, from pre-training to base classes, the ratio varies from one dataset to the other (COCO: 60 unique base classes, 20 unique novel classes, respectively for VOC: 15 base; 5 novel). 
At test time:
Yes, one novel class corresponds to one template for k=1. For k=10 we use 10 templates instead of 1 for the same class. Increasing the number of templates does help (see Table 1 and 2).

We hope that we addressed all your concerns. We are more than happy to provide any additional details should you wish so and we hope you will update the score accordingly.
